source.title: Disentangling the Factors of Convergence between Brains and Computer Vision Models
source.authors: Jos'ephine Raugel; Marc Szafraniec; Huy V. Vo; Camille Couprie; Patrick Labatut; P. Bojanowski; Valentin Wyart; Jean-R'emi King

record.tranche_reason: The study measures how individual vision models align with human brain activity. It does not measure representational similarity between models or test any listed claim version.
record.gate_note: The reported results concern model-to-brain similarity, a related but different construct from model-to-model convergence. The paper cites the Platonic Representation Hypothesis, but its own measurements do not establish whether different models become more similar to one another.
record.test_reason: The study measures model-to-brain similarity (ridge encoding, spatial and temporal hierarchy scores) for DINOv3 variants against fMRI and MEG. It never measures similarity between models. It cites the Platonic Representation Hypothesis only as motivation. Model-to-brain alignment is a related but different construct, so its findings go under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors also stress a developmental chronology: models align first with early sensory cortex and later with prefrontal areas. This order tracks cortical expansion, thickness, myelination and timescales.
record.recipe_differences: Not a test of the original model-to-model convergence method; it uses linear encoding analyses to compare vision-model activations with brain recordings.
record.method_sensitivity: Model-to-brain scores vary with model size, training amount, image type, brain region, and temporal window.

fits_no_version.finding: DINOv3 encoding scores against fMRI and MEG rise with model size (Small 0.096 to Giant 0.107) and with training (R=.03 to .09).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Within a self-supervised vision family, larger and longer-trained models align more closely with human brain responses.

fits_no_version.finding: Matched DINOv3 Large models trained on human-centric images score higher on brain encoding, spatial and temporal scores than models trained on cellular or satellite images. All three improve with training.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The training image domain shapes model-brain alignment. Human-centric data gives the strongest alignment, while other natural images still give partial early-visual alignment.

fits_no_version.finding: Brain-region half times during training correlate with distance from V1 (R=0.91) and with cortical expansion (R=0.88), thickness and myelin.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Models acquire brain-like representations of sensory areas before those of associative or prefrontal areas.

record.problems: The study tests only one family of self-supervised vision models, as the authors note. Its brain measurements are population-level fMRI and MEG, and its results concern model-to-brain alignment rather than pairwise model convergence. Several comparisons are described without numerical scores in the text.
record.rows_left_out: The paper also reports spatial and temporal score trends across size and image type, and region-specific results; these are not individually extracted where the text gives no assignable numerical values beyond the reported comparisons.

untested.parts: No pairwise similarity between independently trained models. Size effects are on brain alignment only, within one family.
No model-to-model mapping or stitching. The linear maps go from model to brain.
No feature or circuit recurrence across models.
Metric and input dependence is not examined for model-to-model similarity.
The data-type manipulation affects brain alignment, not inter-model alignment.

missing.what: Half-time ordering across ROIs and time windows, and correlations with cortical properties (expansion R=0.88, myelin R=-0.85, etc.). These are relevant to model-brain fits only, not to any version.

record.verdict_notes: The study is a brain-model study with no model-to-model similarity. The record's T6/discusses classification and its all-'none' row links are correct.

versions.untested_parts: No pairwise alignment between independently trained models is measured.
No vision-language model comparison or paired image-caption alignment is measured.
No comparison across random seeds or shared features between seed-trained networks is measured.
No mapping, stitching, relative-representation, or unpaired interchangeability between models is tested.
No recurrence of interpretable features or circuits across models is tested.
Similarity metrics and image types are varied for model-to-brain alignment, not for model-to-model convergence or its dependence on metrics and inputs.
The study varies training data and reports model-to-brain alignment, but does not test whether model-to-model alignment is incomplete or whether shared data/objectives explain it.

relation.reason: The introduction discusses universal representational principles and cites Huh et al. as motivation, while the experiments measure brain correspondence.

tranche.reason: The study measures model-to-brain correspondence, a related construct outside the listed claim versions; it neither tests nor uses model-to-model convergence.

source_check.notes: The developmental chronology and cortical-property associations in the recorded authors' conclusion are supported. The extracted '105 training steps' has ambiguous exponent formatting and should not be treated as a verified literal count.
